title: the mudras
hook: a right hand with two fingers folded down, resting at the nose, opening one side and closing the other
carry: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras and the silent teacher: thumb and first finger joined in chin mudra, a lecture made of silence. In a conversation, did you say less and let a gesture carry the rest? Today closes the week. Day one thousand thirty-six.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `CHIN MUDRA: THE LECTURE IS SILENCE.`

segments.voice: A right hand, lifted to the face. The first two fingers are folded down into the palm. The thumb rests against one side of the nose, the ring finger against the other. Someone sitting very straight, eyes closed, presses gently with the thumb, and the breath goes in through the left side only. Then the ring finger closes the left, the thumb lifts, and the breath goes out through the right. Back and forth, slow as a tide. So far this week's mudras have greeted, offered and taught. Today, a mudra with a job: it steers the breath.
screen: `TWO FINGERS FOLDED DOWN.` → `THUMB ON ONE SIDE, RING FINGER ON THE OTHER.` → `A MUDRA THAT STEERS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The practice is alternate-nostril breathing, and the Hatha Yoga Pradipika describes it in its second chapter, in paraphrase: breathe in through the left nostril, then out through the right. Breathe in through the right, then out through the left. The text calls the channels of the subtle body nadis, and says this is how they're made clean. The text's version also holds the breath between in and out, which teachers say to learn in person. The hand shape isn't spelled out in that passage. Teachers supply it, and in some lineages it's called Vishnu mudra: the index and middle fingers folded down, the thumb and ring finger free to open and close the two sides. Others rest those two fingers on the brow instead. Either way, the hand becomes a valve. It's a different kind of mudra from the ones earlier this week. Anjali says something to someone. Chin mudra shows something in silence. This one does something. It's a seal in the most practical sense, closing one side so the breath has only one way to go. Now look back at the week. Darshan, the gaze that meets the deity and is met. The Gita's gaze at the tip of the nose, a point you carry everywhere. The even gaze, seeing the same in all. Then the hands took over. The mudra as a seal, a shape pressed in so it holds. Anjali, the joined palms, a bow to you. Chin mudra, the small self bending to the great, under a banyan tree. And today, the breathing hand. The eyes learned to rest. The hands learned to speak, and now to steer.
screen: `IN THROUGH ONE SIDE, OUT THROUGH THE OTHER.` · `FINGERS FOLDED, THUMB AND RING FINGER FREE.` · `A MUDRA THAT DOES SOMETHING.` · `THIS WEEK: EYES TO REST, HANDS TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `THE HAND BECOMES A VALVE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright. Fold the first two fingers of the right hand into the palm. Close the right nostril gently with the thumb and breathe in, slowly, through the left. Close the left with the ring finger, lift the thumb, and breathe out through the right. Breathe in through the right. Close it, open the left, breathe out through the left. That's one round. Keep it slow and easy, no holding, no forcing. If the nose is blocked or anything feels uncomfortable, simply rest the hand and breathe normally. The bell holds the time.
The mudras. Today, the breathing hand: two fingers folded, the thumb and ring finger opening one side and closing the other.

Your line: steering the breath, one nostril, then the other. Today, notice once what your hands are saying without a word, clenched, open, folded, busy, and let them say something gentler. Day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: In hatha yoga, practitioners do alternate-nostril breathing with the right hand, folding the first two fingers and using the thumb and ring finger to close each side in turn; breath retention is learned from a teacher.

close the left and breathe out through the right.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: nadi, a channel. In hatha yoga, the channels of the subtle body that alternate-nostril breathing is said to clean.

trapdoor: what you thought: mudras are only symbols.

what a scholar hears: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.7–2.10 on nāḍī-śodhana, with the hand shape supplied by later teachers.
